title: Nothing is impossible (Luke 1:26–38)
hookLine: Mary asks how, and hears: with God nothing shall be impossible

lines: THE SIXTH MONTH, THE SAME ANGEL.
NAZARETH: NEVER IN THE OLD TESTAMENT.
cards: In the sixth month of Elisabeth's pregnancy, Luke says, the same angel is sent somewhere completely different. Not the capital, not the holy place, not to a priest.

To Nazareth, a village in Galilee the Old Testament never mentions. To a young woman named Mary, engaged to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. Luke doesn't give her age, or say what she was doing.
Cooking, maybe. Fetching water. Ordinary hours in an ordinary house.
Yesterday an old priest in the temple. Today a young woman in a village nobody's heard of. And her message is far stranger than his.

teach.h: HAIL: THE LORD IS WITH THEE.
teach.b: Gabriel's greeting, in the King James Bible: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women."

She's troubled, Luke says, and turns the words over, wondering what kind of greeting this is. Then the news: she will bear a son, name him Jesus, he will be called the Son of the Highest, and his kingdom will have no end.
Mary asks: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Notice the difference. Zechariah asked, how can I be sure?
Mary asks, how will this happen? Not proof. Just how.
Gabriel answers: the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee.

teach.h: ELISABETH: THE SIGN SHE CAN SEE.
teach.b: Then a sign she can go and see: her relative Elisabeth, the one called barren, is six months along. And then: "For with God nothing shall be impossible."
The Greek can also be read as no word from God will be without power.

teach.h: BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.
teach.b: And Mary's answer: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." Then the angel leaves. Christians across the churches treasure this scene and honor Mary in different ways.

teach.h: WITH GOD NOTHING SHALL BE IMPOSSIBLE.
teach.b: Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor her with special devotion as the Mother of God; the Hail Mary prayer opens with Gabriel's greeting. Many Protestant Christians honor her as a model of trusting faith.
All of them hear a yes in her last line.

how: Many churches celebrate the Annunciation on March 25, nine months before Christmas; Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray the Hail Mary, which begins with Gabriel's greeting, and many Christians read this passage in Advent.

o: the angel sent to both Zechariah and Mary
the angel who guarded Eden's gate with a sword
the name Mary was told to give her son

games.q: what's inside Luke 1:26–38 — tap the pairs.
p: a village never named in the Old Testament

s: he never gives it. he says only that she was a young woman engaged to Joseph.
Mary asked how, and was not struck silent
Zechariah asked how he could be sure; Mary asked how it would happen.
all churches honor Mary in the same way
Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor her with special devotion; many Protestants honor her as a model of faith.

games.q: you're Mary. an angel has told you something impossible, and given you a sign. what do you say?
o: behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.
games.why: her answer is a yes: "be it unto me according to thy word." then the angel departs.

practice: Hold something in your life that looks impossible, a relationship beyond repair, an illness, a habit you can't break, someone you love who seems unreachable, honestly, the way you'd hold something heavy in both hands; Mary didn't pretend, she asked how.
Then loosen your grip a little. If you pray, bring it to God, and if the words fit, say Mary's line: be it unto me according to thy word; if not, hold it open, without forcing an answer.

wordCard.voice: Gabriel. The angel who told Mary that with God nothing is impossible, and that no word from him lacks power.

orig.note: Greek: a word, a thing spoken. Luke 1:37 can be read: no word from God will be without power.

carryVoice: Your line: be it unto me. Not whether, but how. Day five hundred five, done.
